Public Comment: The public is encouraged to address City Council on any matter listed on the agenda or on any other
matter within its jurisdiction subject to the rules of decorum described in Section 2.08.020 of the Norwalk Municipal Code.
If you wish to address City Council, please complete the card that is provided at the rear entrance to Council Chambers
and hand the card to the Sergeant at Arms. City Council will hear public comment on items listed on the agenda during
discussion of the matter and prior to a vote. City Council will hear public comment on matters not listed on the agenda
during the Oral Communications period.

Pursuant to provisions of the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the agenda, or unless
certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The City Council may direct staff to investigate and/or schedule certain
matters for consideration at a future City Council meeting.

Please adhere to the following procedures when addressing the City Council:
   Comments should be limited to 3 minutes or less.
   Comments should be directed to the City Council as a whole and not directed to individual Councilmembers.

Americans with Disabilities Act: In compliance with the ADA, if you need special assistance to participate in a City
meeting or other services offered by this City, please contact the City Clerk’s department, (562) 929-5720. Assisted
listening devices are available at this meeting. Ask the City Clerk if you desire to use this device. Upon request, the agenda
and documents in the agenda packet can be made available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability.
Notification of at least 48 hours prior to the meeting or time when services are needed will assist the City staff in assuring
that reasonable arrangements can be made to provide accessibility to the meeting or service.

Note: Any writings and/or documents provided to a majority of the City Council regarding any item on this agenda after it has been
posted will also be made available for public inspection.

Writings and/or documents are available for inspection in the City Clerk’s Department, City Hall, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard during
regular business hours, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., Monday – Thursday and 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., every other Friday; telephone (562)
929-5720. You may also contact the City Clerk via e-mail at recordsrequests@norwalkca.gov.

  REGULAR MEETING

Mayor Rios called the meeting to order at 6:07 p.m. in the Council Chambers, Norwalk
City Hall, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard, Norwalk, California. Responding to roll call were
Councilmembers Perez and Valencia, Vice Mayor Ayala, and Mayor Rios.
Councilmember Ramirez was absent. Also present were Jesus M. Gomez, City Manager;
Gloria Ramirez, Deputy City Attorney; and Camille Moreno, Assistant City Clerk.

The invocation was delivered by Dr. George Bojorquez, New Creation Church; followed
by the flag salute, led by Evie Gomez, Girl Scouts of Greater Los Angeles.

CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS

Councilmember Perez wished everyone a happy Election Day, announced the polls close
at 8 p.m., encouraged the community to go out and vote; and shared that the Norwalk
Now newsletter is out, in which it highlights the Norwalk Public Safety Department’s 35
years of service. Councilmember Valencia reported on her attendance at the Norwalk
High School Junior Varsity and Varsity softball games and the Norwalk Little League
Opening Day Ceremony. Mayor Rios acknowledged dignitaries in attendance; thanked
staff and residents for the success of the E-Waste/Shred-a-thon event; and reported on
her attendance at the Read Across America event; invited everyone to the upcoming Meet
the Mayor event at El Baja Grill, as well as the ribbon cutting ceremony at New River Park
for the new playground on March 11.

SPECIAL PRESENTATIONS

City Council presented a proclamation declaring March as National Red Cross Month in
the City of Norwalk, accepted by Chris Sanchez, National Red Cross.

City Council recognized the Norwalk Lady Vikings for winning the Jamz Nationals Cheer
and Dance Championship.

City Council presented a proclamation declaring March as Women’s History Month in the
City of Norwalk, accepted by Norma Amezcua, Norwalk-La Mirada Unified School District.

CITY MANAGER COMMENTS

A video was shared highlighting the “Bi-Weekly Review.”

RESOLUTION NO. 24-13 - APPROVING THE TERMINATION OF THE FRONT
STREET PARTICIPATION AGREEMENT - City Council

a. found that the proposed action is exempt from the requirements of the California
  Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) in accordance with CEQA Guidelines Section
  15061(b)(3) under common sense exemption which provides that CEQA applies only
  to projects which have the potential for causing a significant effect on the environment.
  Where it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the activity in
  question may have a significant effect on the environment, the activity is not subject
  to CEQA;

b. adopted Resolution No. 24-13, A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE
  CITY OF NORWALK APPROVING THE TERMINATION OF THE FRONT STREET
  PARTICIPATION AGREEMENT, which does not authorize any specific development;

02 AND CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT NO. 2023-05 - 11642 FIRESTONE BOULEVARD

Mayor Rios opened the public hearing to consider the appeal of the Planning
Commission’s denial of the Precise Development Plan No. 2023-02 and Conditional Use
Permit No. 2023-05 for 11642 Firestone Boulevard. The Assistant City Clerk presented
a report on legal requisites for notice of hearing. Following a report presented by Jill Ann
Arabe, Development Services Manager, the applicant Andrew Miliotis spoke and
presented a letter in opposition of the matter. Dora Sandoval testified in person in
opposition of the project, and the Assistant City Clerk shared that an email was submitted
by Steve Contreras in opposition of the project. There being no other persons wishing to
testify in this matter, Mayor Rios closed the public hearing. Councilmember Perez moved
and Vice Mayor Ayala seconded to adopt Resolution No. 24-02, A RESOLUTION OF
THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF NORWALK SETTING FORTH ITS FINDINGS

SUBJECT:  FEDERAL  TRANSIT  ADMINISTRATION  CERTIFICATIONS  AND
  ASSURANCES FOR FEDERAL FISCAL YEAR 2024

Background:

The City’s Transportation Department develops and submits applications for Federal Transit
Administration (FTA) Capital and/or Formula grant funding in keeping with the acquisition of
replacement buses, facility construction/rehabilitation, preventative maintenance, associated
major bus components, etc. An element of the grant approval process requires applicants to
provide Certifications and Assurances (C&A’s) for FTA regulatory compliance on an annual
basis.

The C&A’s cover multiple compliance areas such as assurances concerning applicable Federal
regulations; Civil Rights, Procurement, Lobbying, Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA),
Drug/Alcohol testing, etc. This year’s C&A certifies the role of a Safety Committee comprised of
frontline workers in the development of Norwalk Transit’s Public Transportation Agency Safety
Plan (PTASP), which was previously approved by Council on December 6, 2022.

Also, the City is required to designate a representative to affirm compliance with the C&A’s as a
part of the grant application process. In prior FTA grant applications, the Executive Director of
Regional Transportation, as a designee of the City Manager, has signed the FTA C&A’s
Affirmation of Applicant on behalf of the City along with Affirmation of Applicant’s Attorney signed
by the City Attorney.

SUBJECT:  NORWALK TRANSIT SYSTEM TITLE VI 2024 COMPLIANCE UPDATE

Background:

In keeping with United States Department of Transportation (USDOT) 49 Code of Federal
Regulations (CFR) Section 21.9(b) and Federal Transit Administration (FTA); Norwalk Transit
System (NTS) must submit a Federal Transit Administration (FTA) Title VI Program update once
every three (3) years to demonstrate that all transit services and related benefits are distributed
in an equitable manner.

Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 provides that “No person in the United States shall, on the
grounds of race, color, or national origin, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits
of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial
assistance”.

Pursuant to FTA Circular 4702.1B – Title VI Guidelines for FTA Recipients; updates must include
the following information:

1. A summary of public outreach and involvement activities undertaken since the last Title VI
submission and a description of steps taken to ensure that minority and low-income people had
meaningful access to these activities.

2. A copy of the agency’s plan that includes an outreach plan, for providing language
assistance for minorities, and limited English proficiency populations, that was based on the
Department of Transportation (DOT) Limited English Proficiency (LEP) Guidance.

3.  NTS complaint procedures and guidelines for filing Title VI complaints.

4. A list of any public transportation related Title VI investigations, complaints, or lawsuits filed
with the agency since the time of the last submission.

5. A copy of the agency’s Tittle VI notice to the public that indicates the agency complies with
Title VI and informs members of the public of protections against discrimination afforded to them
by Title VI, as well as instructions to the public on how to file a discrimination complaint, including
a copy of the complaint form.

6.  Information regarding the racial breakdown of transit-related policy boards or committees.

7. An equity analysis indicating if the recipient has constructed a facility (such as a garage,
maintenance facility, or operation center) since the last Title VI assessment.

8. A copy of board meeting minutes, resolution, or other appropriate documentation showing
the board of directors or appropriate governing entity or official(s) responsible for policy decisions
reviewed and approved the Title VI Program.

9.  System-wide standards and policies that address:

  a) Vehicle load
  b) Vehicle headway
  c) On-time performance
  d) Service availability

10.  Service policies that address

  a) Provision of transit amenities
  b) Vehicle assignment

These requirements and guidelines apply to all FTA recipients. FTA is responsible for ensuring
that its recipients fully comply with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Therefore, this program
renewal addresses all compliance requirements and includes needed updates to the required
elements of the Title VI Program.

Fiscal Impact:

There is no impact on the General Fund. Approval of this report is needed to support the
Department’s annual request for FTA Section 5307 funds to support capital projects and
operating expenditures.

 Introduction
Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 is a federal law that prohibits recipients and subrecipients of Federal
financial assistance (e.g., states, local governments, transit providers) from discriminating on the basis of
race, color, or national origin in their programs or activities, and obligates Federal funding agencies to
enforce compliance.

Under Title VI, the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) has the responsibility to provide oversight of
recipients and to enforce their compliance with Title VI, ensuring that recipients do not use DOT funds to
subsidize discrimination based on race, color, or national origin.

Norwalk Transit System (NTS) is a recipient of Federal Transit Administration (FTA) funds and has prepared
this report in accordance with FTA Circular 4702.1B, dated October 1, 2012.

NTS operates local fixed-route transit service as a department of the City of Norwalk. NTS’ route network
includes six routes that provide fixed-route service in the cities of Norwalk, Artesia, Bellflower, Cerritos,
La Mirada, Santa Fe Springs, Whittier, South El Monte, El Monte, La Habra, and portions of unincorporated
Los Angeles County including Los Nietos and Avocado Heights. Exhibit 1 shows a map of NTS, which
includes:

Route 1 (Rio Hondo/Bellflower) – Primarily a north-southwesterly route between the City of Bellflower
on its southern end to the unincorporated Los Angeles County community of Avocado Heights at its
northern end, this route also serves Norwalk, Bellflower, Santa Fe Springs, Los Nietos, West Whittier and
Whittier. The Norwalk Civic Center and Entertainment Complex, Rio Hondo College, and Cerritos College
are among the major destinations on this route. Route 1 operates seven days a week. The span of service
is 5:20 a.m. to 10:36 p.m. on weekdays. Weekend service is from 7:52 a.m. to 5:33 p.m. The service
frequency is approximately every 30 minutes on weekdays and approximately every 50 minutes on
weekends.

Route 2 (Norwalk Square/Metro C Line/Cerritos College/Cerritos Mall) – Provides circulation within the
cities of Norwalk, Cerritos, and Artesia via a bidirectional loop. Important destinations include the
Norwalk Civic Center area, the I-605/I-105 Metro C Line Station, Cerritos College, and Los Cerritos Center.
This route operates seven days a week. The span of service is between 5:55 a.m. and 7:33 p.m. on
weekdays. On weekends the route operates between 9:16 a.m. and 6:44 p.m. Service frequency is
approximately every 37 minutes in each direction on weekdays and approximately one hour 74 minutes
on weekends.

Route 3 (Whittier Depot/Alondra & Norwalk Blvd.) – Connects Norwalk and Cerritos at its southern end
with the City of Whittier at its northern terminus, also serving Santa Fe Springs. The Norwalk Civic Center
area, downtown Whittier, Gateway Plaza Center, Santa Fe Springs City Hall, and several high schools are
among major destinations on this route. Route 3 operates five days a week with no service on the
weekend. It operates from 5:29 a.m. to 7:29 p.m. on weekdays providing 60-minute headways throughout
the day.

Route 4 (Imperial Highway/Metro C Line Station/Norwalk Metrolink Station) – Is an east-west route
along Imperial Highway between the I-605/I-105 Metro C Line Station and Beach Boulevard in Orange
County. This route provides connections to Metrolink at the Norwalk/Santa Fe Springs Metrolink Station.

 Route 5 (Rosecrans/Metro C Line Station/City of La Mirada) – Operates primarily along Rosecrans
Avenue between the I-605/I-105 Metro C Line Station in Norwalk and the city of La Mirada, also serving
Santa Fe Springs. The service operates five days a week with no service on weekends and connects the
Metro C Line Station with both residential and industrial land uses on Rosecrans Avenue. It operates from
4:15 a.m. to 7:40 p.m. on weekdays providing 45-minute headways throughout the day.

Route 7 (C Line Station/El Monte Bus Station) – Operates along various streets between the I-605/I-105
Metro C Line Station in Norwalk and the El Monte Bus Station in the city of El Monte, also serving Santa
Fe Springs, Whittier, and South El Monte. The service operates six days a week with no service on Sunday.
This route was formerly part of Metro Line 270. It operates from 3:48 a.m. to 8:51 p.m. on weekdays
providing 56- to 60-minute frequency along the entire route throughout the day and 20-to-30-minute
headways between the El Monte Bus Station and Rio Hondo College. Saturday service operates between
5:49 a.m. and 7:57 p.m. every 60 minutes.

NTS fixed-route service utilizes 34 buses including 25 CNG Gilligs, six BEB Gilligs, and three hybrid New
Flyers. The peak-vehicle requirement is 20 buses, with the remainder serving as spares. NTS provides
services to nearly 800,000 passengers per year within a service area of 637,365 residents.

In addition to fixed-route service, NTS provides a high-quality and efficient demand-responsive service
(Dial-A-Ride) for Norwalk’s senior and disabled residents within the jurisdictional boundaries of the City
of Norwalk. NTS also contracts for late evening weekday supplemental taxi voucher service and daytime

Public Participation Plan
Promoting inclusive public participation is an important element of a transit agency’s Title VI program.
Recipients have wide latitude to determine how, when, and how often specific public participation
activities should take place, and which specific measures are most appropriate. The Title VI guidelines
suggest that a recipient’s public participation plan for minority populations may be part of efforts that
extend more broadly to include other constituencies that are traditionally underserved, such as people
with disabilities, low-income populations, and others.

The Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) is the metropolitan planning organization
(MPO) for the six-county Southern California region, including the counties of Imperial, Los Angeles,
Orange, San Bernardino, Riverside, and Ventura. From the beaches to the high desert, the six-county
region that encompasses Southern California spans 38,000 square miles, 191 cities and a population of
over 19 million. The SCAG region is among the largest and most diverse in the world, with a unique
combination of languages, ethnicities and cultures.

SCAG is responsible for developing long range transportation, and environmental plans for the region.
Norwalk Transit relies on SCAG’s Public Participation Plan to ensure compliance with applicable Tittle VI
regulations when embarking in a project that has regional impact.

However, for projects that only impact the Norwalk Transit service area, the agency has its own Public
Participation processes. In an effort to provide equal access to services provided by NTS, and promote
inclusive public participation, the City of Norwalk advises its citizens of proposed changes to service, and
fares through notification of the Public Hearing published in the Whittier Daily News, Mid Valley News,
and La Opinion. Letters are mailed to stakeholders, and notices are posted on Norwalk Transit System
buses. Finally, Norwalk transportation staff meets with the San Gabriel Valley and Gateway Cities Service
Councils in order to encourage feedback from the public, and ensure their concerns are addressed.

Limited English Proficiency Plan
Individuals who have a limited ability to read, write, speak or understand English are Limited English
Proficient or “LEP” as defined in the FTA Title VI regulations. This LEP Plan implements Federal policy
guidance regarding responsibilities to Limited English Proficient persons for NTS.

The analysis provided in this report has been developed in order to ensure that NTS provides language
assistance to LEP persons. The following section reports the results of the “Four Factor Analysis” included
in FTA Circular 4702.1B. The below section develops the Language Assistance Plan for NTS.

The analysis that follows has been completed to identify areas where NTS can expect to encounter LEP
individuals in its operation of transit services and to determine whether NTS’ efforts are sufficient to
ensure that LEP individuals are not prevented from using public transportation services. The analysis uses
data from the 2022 five-year American Community Survey, which has the largest sample size and most
reliable data of any current source.

Title VI Program Update FY 2024  11
 The Four Factor Analysis
The Four Factor Analysis is used to determine the specific language services that are appropriate to
provide to ensure meaningful access to programs and activities. A careful analysis helps to determine the
effectiveness of communication with LEP persons and informs language access planning. The Four Factors
and the associated steps are:

Factor 1: The number or proportion of LEP persons eligible to be served or likely to be encountered by
the program or recipient.

USDOT guidance for this first factor says, “The greater the number or proportion of LEP persons from a
particular language group served or encountered in the eligible service population, the more likely
language services are needed.”

How LEP individuals interact with NTS

Major points of contact with LEP individuals are the Customer Service Lobby, either in-person or via
phone, and on fixed-route buses and dial-a-ride vans.

Identification of LEP communities, and assessing the number or proportion of LEP persons from each
language group to determine the appropriate language services for each language group

The U.S. Census Bureau compiles data in its decennial Census and American Community Survey (ACS).
Among the data collected is information on primary language spoken at home and the ability to speak
English. Categories include whether individuals indicate they speak English “very well” or “less than very
well.” The LEP population consists of those individuals who speak other languages AND speak English
“less than very well.”

Exhibit 7 shows information on the LEP population in the NTS service area. The number of residents age
five and older who speak English less than “very well” is 108,965, or 21.5 percent of the total population.
Spanish is the primary language spoken in the NTS service area other than English. Spanish-speaking
residents who speak English less than very well account for 14.4% percent of the total population.

The FTA Title VI guidance refers to the US Department of Justice Safe Harbor Provision, which has been
adopted by USDOT. The Safe Harbor Provision stipulates that “if a recipient provides written translation
of vital documents for each eligible LEP language group that constitutes five percent or 1,000 persons,
whichever is less, of the total population of persons eligible to be served or likely to be affected or
encountered, then such action will be considered strong evidence of compliance with the recipient’s
written translation obligations.” Under this provision, NTS would offer strong evidence of compliance
with LEP requirements if it provides translations of its vital documents into:

  •  Spanish (73,097 LEP residents, or 14.40% of the population)
  •  Chinese (10,826 LEP residents, or 2.13% of the population)
  •  Korean (8,840 LEP residents, or 1.74% of the population)
  •  Tagalog (4,880 LEP residents, or 0.96% of the population)
  •  Vietnamese (4,045 LEP residents, or 0.80% of the population)

 Literacy Skills of LEP populations
Norwalk Transit System has no direct evidence of the literacy skills of LEP populations in their native
languages. In the absence of such evidence, translation of documents is assumed to be an effective
practice.

Whether LEP persons are underserved due to language barriers
NTS has no direct evidence of language barriers resulting in the LEP population being underserved. As
Exhibit 7 shows, the primary language spoken by the LEP population is Spanish. All key documents are
currently provided in Spanish. Both customer service representative and coach operators indicated the
most common language they encounter is Spanish. On the rare occasions when there is call or visit from
someone who speaks another language, it is the City’s practice to summon a staff employee who speaks
this language. However, there have been some LEP individuals who do not speak Spanish who have faced
barriers to using NTS due to limited English proficiency (see Factor 2).

Factor 2: The frequency with which LEP individuals come into contact with the program.

The Federal guidance for this factor recommends that agencies should assess major points of contact with
LEP individuals.

Use of bus and dial-a-ride service
Use of the City’s bus service is a major point of contact with LEP individuals, since non-users do not
typically come into contact with NTS. Dial-a-ride service is also an important point of contact with LEP
individuals.

Purchase of passes and tickets through vending machines, outlets, websites, and over the phone
Pass purchase is a point of contact with LEP individuals. NTS offers Metro Tokens, EZ Transit passes and
Transit Access pass (TAP) cards for sale.

Participation in public meetings
Public meetings are an occasional point of contact with LEP individuals. NTS holds public meetings
infrequently, generally during major studies or to present proposed changes to the bus network. NTS will
continue its efforts to track participation by LEP individuals.

Customer service interactions
Customer service interactions are frequent points of contact with LEP individuals. Customer service
personnel report daily contact with LEP individuals, as noted in Factor 1. The overwhelming majority of
these daily contacts are with Spanish-speaking individuals.

Ridership surveys
Ridership surveys are an occasional point of contact with LEP individuals, for the same reason as
participation in public meetings: NTS does not routinely conduct ridership surveys. The most recent on-
board survey (2012) was conducted in English and Spanish and did not include question about other
languages. In the future, should the City conduct another ridership survey, a question regarding language
spoken and preference will be included.

Operator surveys
NTS conducted a survey of its customer-facing personnel in February 2024 during the preparation of this
Title VI Program Update. Staff were asked a series of questions regarding their observations and

Title VI Program Update FY 2024  16
 experience specific to LEP individuals they encountered through their work at NTS. A total of 53 drivers
and other staff members responded to the survey. Nearly all of them (92.5 percent) identified Spanish as
the primary language they encounter, followed by Chinese (26.4 percent), Korean (17 percent),
Vietnamese (11.3 percent), Tagalog (5.7 percent), and Arabic (5.7 percent). Other languages cited by one
individual each were Thai, Hindi, and American Sign Language (ASL).

The survey asked drivers/coach operators to indicate how many unique riders they encountered each
week that did not speak English or did not speak English very well. More than 60 percent said they had
more than 10 such encounters per week. Only two respondents indicated no encounters with LEP
individuals. Among dispatchers/customer service representatives, 34.3 percent indicated having more
than 10 encounters per week (either via phone or in person), while 38.6 percent had between five and
10, and 37.1 percent had less than five or none.

While only 41.5 percent of respondents cited at least a basic knowledge of another language, 62.3 percent
indicated having no issues or problems communicating with LEP individuals. Another 35.9 percent
indicated having only occasional problems. Most respondents who indicated some level of knowledge in
another language (whether basic or fluent) spoke Spanish (35.9 percent), though others cited American

More than half of respondents noted that translated service brochures or onboard notices in other
languages would be beneficial. The most common information requested by LEP individuals is basic
directions or instructions. One respondent indicated a lack of Spanish-speaking customer service staff on
Saturdays.

Stakeholder surveys
NTS also conducted a survey of community stakeholders in February 2024 during the preparation of this
Title VI Program Update. Stakeholders were identified based on their location (serving the NTS service
area) as well as their programs (e.g., serving populations that were likely to speak other languages and/or
have limited English proficiency). Seventy-eight stakeholders were contacted by email inviting them to
take the short survey either online or by returning a form-fillable .pdf survey via email.

Two completed surveys were received. The first was from the Sahara organization, which serves a
population of more than 50 individuals, many of whom have limited English proficiency and use Norwalk
Transit Systems. These individuals speak Hindi, Gujurati, and Punjabi, and primarily have difficulty
scheduling dial-a-ride appointments due to a language barrier. If they speak to someone who speaks their
language, they have no trouble scheduling a ride.

The second survey was submitted by Holy Family Catholic Church, which serves individuals speaking
Spanish, Chinese, Portuguese, and Tagalog. Many of its parishioners are elderly, and speaking in fluent
English makes them uncomfortable. The respondent indicated that language is a barrier to using NTS, but
was not sure how many parishioners use the service. They also indicated that most non-native English
speakers in the parish speak English very well.

These two stakeholders, though they provide only a snapshot of small populations within the NTS service
area, reinforce the importance of the role NTS plays in the community and with LEP individuals. The
stakeholder survey instrument and a full list of the stakeholders contacted is provided in Appendix F.

 The results for Factor 2 indicate daily contact with Spanish-speaking individuals and less frequent contact
with LEP individuals speaking Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, Tagalog, and Arabic. This PPP (Section 4)
proposes strategies to improve contact.

Factor 3: The nature and importance of the program, activity, or service provided to people’s lives.

The Federal guidance assumes that the provision of public transportation is a vital service, especially for
people without access to a vehicle and for persons with disabilities. The Federal guidance also notes that
“a coordinated plan to meet the specific transportation needs of seniors and persons with disabilities will
often also meet the needs of LEP persons.”

NTS fixed-route service is the program’s most critical service. NTS also provides dial-a-ride service to
elderly and disabled residents within the City of Norwalk. It should be noted that Access Services provides
the ADA complementary paratransit service throughout Los Angeles County, including within the NTS
service area.

Factor 4: The resources available to the recipient for LEP outreach and associated costs.

The Federal guidance looks to evaluating the proposed improvements against the level of resources
available in an agency’s budget to provide meaningful access for LEP individuals. The guidance notes that
“resource and cost issues can often be reduced by technological advances, reasonable business practices,
and the sharing of language assistance materials and services among and between recipients, advocacy
groups, LEP populations and Federal agencies.”

NTS already makes its complaint procedure and complaint forms available in Spanish, Chinese, and Korean
on its website. Based on the results of the demographic and four-factor analysis, providing this
information in Tagalog and Vietnamese would be warranted, given the size of the LEP populations in the
service area and the reported encounters of these languages by NTS staff. Translating the complaint
procedure and complaint forms into two additional languages would be a one-time cost. Including a
sentence regarding the availability of Title VI information in those languages on the Notice to the Public,
with a phone number to call, could mitigate the need to have separate Notice to the Public documents in
all identified languages. Other key documents, including the Dial-A-Ride and TaxiCard applications, would
also need to be translated. This would also be a one-time cost for each translation.

NTS has 34 individuals who speak Spanish and can assist with Spanish translations, one who speaks
Chinese and can assist with translations, and one individual who speaks another (unspecified) language.
The City has one individual who speaks Korean and can assist with translation, and 128 individuals who
speak another (unspecified) language. The current operations contractor includes six Spanish-speaking
staff as well as individuals who speak Portuguese, French, and Arabic. In addition, coach operators
responding to the survey also indicated speaking at least basic Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean, and Tagalog.

While providing service information in multiple languages can be cost-prohibitive for a small transit
agency, ensuring access to information is essential. The Norwalk Transit Systems website includes a
Google Translate widget that enables the site to be translated into multiple languages, including those
listed herein. This is effective with website text, though less so with graphics or linked files. Linked .pdf
route schedules are provided in English and Spanish, regardless of which language the site is being viewed
in. Website graphics (including those promoting new bus schedules, real-time route information, and bus
operator recruitment) are in English only. Including such information as part of the website text (rather

The current practice in the event of a call from an individual who does not speak English or Spanish is to
summon a worker who speaks that language. NTS also encourages community groups to provide an

Language Assistance Plan
In this section, the results of the Four Factor Analysis are used to determine which language assistance
services are appropriate. The resulting Language Assistance Plan clearly addresses the identified needs of
the LEP populations served by NTS.

The Language Assistance Plan contains five elements:

  1.  Description of LEP populations served, based on the Four Factor Analysis
  2.  Providing Language Assistance Services by Language
  3.  Providing Notice to LEP Persons
  4.  Monitoring and Updating the LEP Plan
  5.  Training Employees

Description of LEP Populations Served
This element relies on the results of the Four Factor analysis. DOT’s Safe Harbor Provision stipulates that,
if a recipient provides written translation of vital documents for each eligible LEP language group that
constitutes five percent or 1,000 persons, whichever is less, of the total population of persons eligible to
be served or likely to be affected or encountered, then such action will be considered strong evidence of
compliance with the recipient’s written translation obligations. The City has identified the number and
proportion of LEP individuals within its service area using data from the 2022 American Community Survey
five-year estimates. Under this provision, eligible LEP language groups include:

  •  Spanish
  •  Chinese
  •  Korean
  •  Vietnamese
  •  Tagalog

Providing Language Assistance Services by Language
NTS will print its key information in transit documents in English, Spanish, Korean, Chinese, Vietnamese,
and Tagalog to address the community’s needs. Key information includes Title VI documents, route
schedules, application for eligibility for Norwalk Transit System Senior and Disabled Transit, TaxiCard
application, notice advising LEP individuals of free language assistance, and all service and fare change
notifications. NTS will also ensure that its Customer Service representatives have language skills (or access
to language skills) in these five languages that allow them to communicate with LEP individuals.

Providing Notice to LEP Persons
Federal guidance provides that once an agency has decided that it will provide language services, it is
important that the agency notify LEP persons of services available free of charge. Suggested methods as
to how an agency can provide such information include posting signs in intake areas or entry points,
stating in outreach documents that language services are available; using an automated telephone voice
mail attendant or menu system.

NTS will include a statement in all route brochures/schedules in Spanish, Korean, Chinese, Tagalog, and
Vietnamese regarding the availability of key documents in that language, availability of translation
services at the customer service number, and availability of translation services on its website.

Monitoring and Updating the LEP Plan
Per the FTA’s requirements, the City’s Title VI Program shall be updated at least once every three years.
In between update cycles, NTS will monitor the LEP Plan by the following methods:

  •  Keeping a log of customer service interactions in languages other than English, by language
  spoken;
  •  Reviewing the log annually to track emerging LEP populations that may need translation of key
  documents;
  •  Reviewing the LEP Plan when census updates are released;
  •  Seeking advice from community groups representing LEP populations regarding the best ways to
  communicate; and
  •  Meeting upon request with groups representing other LEP populations.

  •  How to handle a potential Title VI/LEP complaint.

Service Standards
Federal Title VI guidelines require all fixed-route transit providers to set service standards and policies for
each fixed-route mode operated to guard against discriminatory service design or operations decisions.
These standards and policies must address how service is distributed across the transit system, and must
ensure that the manner of the distribution affords users access to these assets.

NTS described transit performance standards for its fixed-route bus network in its previous Title VI update,
including added factors such as on-time performance, and service availability.

Vehicle Load
NTS has established a maximum load standard as 1.5 or 150% of seated capacity. Loads greater than this
should be of short duration (five stops or fewer). NTS examines its peak loads most closely during its
triennial line-by-line analysis, when a complete ride check provides updated information on loads
throughout the network on all days. NTS also monitors peak loads on an ad-hoc basis in response to

Title VI Program Update FY 2024  22
 operator input or passenger complaints. NTS reviews passenger loads when making schedule adjustments
to improve on-time performance.

Vehicle Headway
Service demand, scheduling constraints, fiscal constraints, and capital resources are all considered when
setting headways. The maximum vehicle headway for NTS routes is 90 minutes, with more frequent
service provided according to passenger demand. Current vehicle headways are as follows:

  3  60 minutes  no service

On-Time Performance
The 2012 Comprehensive Operational Analysis for NTS reported on-time performance for all routes on all
days at 64 percent. On-time performance was measured as departing from a timepoint no more than one
minute earlier and no more than five minutes later than the published departure time. When measured
at all timepoints throughout the system, a “typical” on-time performance is in the high 60s to lower 70s
in terms of percentage of all trips, due to the vagaries of traffic (accidents, construction) and the spillover
effect of major delays. At the time of the prior Title VI Program Update, NTS proposed a near-term goal
of 70 percent on-time performance. NTS had intended to complete an updated Comprehensive
Operational Analysis in FY 2023/24, but received no bids, and the project will be re-let in 2024. Modest
changes were made to the routes in January 2024 in an effort to improve on-time performance. More
significant changes, as well as any changes to the on-time performance standard, will be addressed in that
study.

Service Availability
Service availability is a general measure of the distribution of routes within a transit provider’s service
area. NTS’ service area extends well beyond the City of Norwalk, and many other transit operators provide
service within this area. NTS proposes a standard that considers even distribution of service such that 75
percent of residents of the City of Norwalk have access to fixed route bus service within a one-quarter
mile walking distance from their residence and 95 percent have access within one-half mile. Because
Metro service complements NTS service, the NTS will consider both services when setting this
performance standard. As shown in Exhibit 9, 100 percent of Norwalk residents have a fixed route within
one-half mile of their residence.

 Service Policies
FTA guidance requires fixed-route transit providers to develop a policy for the equitable distribution of
transit amenities and for vehicle assignment by route. The following service policies are proposed for
Norwalk Transit System.

Distribution of Transit Amenities
NTS locates bus stops and provides and maintains benches, shelters, signage, and trash receptacles at
these bus stops in close coordination with the local jurisdictions (municipalities or county). Installation of
transit amenities along bus routes are based on numerous factors including the number of passenger
boardings at stops along those routes. The NTS policy regarding distribution of transit amenities
categorizes stops into three tiers:

  •  Tier 1 bus stops typically have 25 or fewer boardings per weekday. Amenities include bench
  seating, signage with lighting, and trash receptacle.

  •  Tier 2 bus stops typically have between 25 and 50 boardings per weekday. Tier 2 bus stops have
  Tier 1 amenities plus passenger shelter structures.

  •  Tier 3 (“Landmark”) bus stops typically have over 50 boardings per weekday. Landmark bus stops
  have Tier 2 amenities along with high visibility, themed or architecturally designed improvements
  that will be constructed at prominent locations in the City of Norwalk.

Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, ridership and typical boardings have been affected. NTS is continuing to
evaluate how this impacts its bus stop development.

Vehicle Assignment
Fixed-route vehicles are randomly assigned from one location. Bus assignments take into account the
operating characteristics of buses of various lengths, which are matched to the operating characteristics
of the route. Routes with lower ridership are assigned smaller buses. Some routes requiring tight turns
on narrow streets may need to be operated with smaller buses. Bus assignments are also rotated to allow
for vehicle maintenance to occur. NTS’ fleet has an average age of 8.15 years as of 2024. Twenty vehicles
are used in peak service and 14 are used as spares. The complete 34-bus inventory is shown in Exhibit 10.

  Guidance for Filing an Administrative Complaint under
  Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964

Title VI is the portion of the 1964 Civil Rights Act that bans discrimination on the basis of race, color, and
national origin in programs and activities that receive federal funds or other forms of federal financial
assistance. Specifically, Title VI provides that “[n]o person in the United States shall, on the ground of race,
color, or national origin, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to
discrimination under any program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” 42 U.S.C. § 2000d. If
you believe that you are excluded from participation in, denied the benefits of, or subjected to
discrimination under any program that receives federal financial assistance, you may file a Title VI
complaint with the office of civil rights at the federal agency that provided the financial assistance.

Who Can File a Complaint?
Title VI prohibits discrimination against “person[s].” One need not be a citizen of the United States to be
protected by the statute.

Information to Include
In your Title VI complaint to the federal agency, you should include:

  1. Your contact information (e.g., phone number, address).
  a. If you are filing on behalf of another person, include your name and contact information,
  and your relation to that person.
  2. The recipient of federal financial assistance that allegedly committed the discriminatory act.
  a. (e.g., Department of Transportation).
  3. A description of the alleged discriminatory conduct including dates.
  a. (e.g.).
  4. A description of how that alleged discriminatory act has the effect of causing a specific adverse
  impact.
  a. An adverse impact is a negative natural consequence of the alleged discriminatory act
  b. (e.g.).
  5. A description of how that adverse impact disparately affects an individual or group on the basis
  one of the categories protected by Title VI (i.e., race, color, or national origin).
  a. Disparity is the comparison of the adverse impacts on the protected class with a non-
  protected class. An allegation of disparity is a necessary component of the complaint.
  b. (e.g.).
  6. A description of any possible retaliation you may have suffered (if any) for complaining about the
  alleged discrimination.
  a. Retaliation refers to any adverse action taken by the entity because you alleged
  discrimination.
  b. (e.g.).
  7. The complaint must be signed and dated.

   Guía para presentar un reclamo administrativo en virtud del
  Título VI de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964

El Título VI es la parte de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 que prohíbe la discriminación por motivos de
raza, color y nacionalidad en programas y actividades que reciben fondos federales u otras formas de
ayuda financiera federal. En particular, el Título VI estipula que a “[n]inguna persona en los Estados
Unidos, debido a su raza, color o nacionalidad, se la discrimine o excluya de participar en cualquier
programa o actividad que recibe ayuda financiera federal, ni se le nieguen sus beneficios”. Sección 2000d
del Código 42 de los Estados Unidos. Si considera que se lo discrimina o excluye de participar en cualquier
programa que recibe ayuda financiera federal, o se le niegan sus beneficios, puede presentar un reclamo
en virtud del Título VI ante la oficina de derechos civiles de la agencia federal que proporcionó la ayuda
financiera.

¿Quién puede presentar un reclamo?
El Título VI prohíbe la discriminación de “persona[s].” No es necesario ser ciudadano de los Estados Unidos
para recibir la protección del estatuto.

Información que incluir
En su reclamo en virtud del Título VI ante la agencia federal, debe incluir:

  1. Su información de contacto (p. ej., número de teléfono, dirección).
  1. Si presenta el reclamo en nombre de otra persona, incluya su nombre e información de contacto
  y su relación con dicha persona.
  2. Beneficiario de ayuda financiera federal que presuntamente cometió el acto discriminatorio.
  a. (P. ej., Departamento de Transporte).
  3. Una descripción de la presunta conducta discriminatoria, con fechas incluidas.
  a. (Ejemplo).
  4. Una descripción de cómo dicho presunto acto discriminatorio provoca un impacto adverso
  específico.
  a. Un impacto adverso es una consecuencia negativa natural del presunto acto
  discriminatorio.
  b. (Ejemplo).
  5. Una descripción de cómo ese impacto adverso afecta de forma dispar a una persona grupo en
  virtud de una de las categorías protegidas por el Título VI (es decir, raza, color o nacionalidad).
  c. Disparidad es la comparación de los impactos adversos en la clase protegida frente a una
  clase no protegida. Una presunción de disparidad es un componente necesario del
  reclamo.
  d. (Ejemplo).
  6. Una descripción de cualquier posible represalia que pudo haber sufrido (si la hubiera) por
  reclamar a raíz de la presunta discriminación.
  a. Represalia se refiere a cualquier acción adversa tomada por la entidad a raíz de su
  denuncia de discriminación.
  b. (Ejemplo).
  7. El reclamo debe estar firmado y fechado.

El reclamo debe presentarse (recibirse) en la oficina de derechos civiles de la agencia federal dentro de
los 180 días posteriores a la conducta discriminatoria, aunque la agencia podría ejercer su discreción y
aceptar un reclamo presentado con posterioridad. Lo mejor es presentarlo dentro del período de 180 días.

  《1964 年公民權利法案》 (Civil Rights Act of 1964) 第 VI 篇所訂立提出行政投訴的指南

第 VI 篇是《1964 年公民權利法案》的一部分，明令禁止在獲得聯邦資金或其他形式聯 邦財
政援助的計畫及活動中，基於種族、膚色與國籍予以歧視的行為。具體而言，第 VI 篇指出「
在美國境內，任何獲得聯邦財政援助的計畫或活動皆『不』得基於種族、膚色與 國籍而不允許
任何人參與、拒絕向其提供福利，或予以歧視」42 U.S.C. § 2000d。若您 認為自己在任何獲得
聯邦財政援助的計畫中遭到排除參與、拒絕福利，或受到歧視，得向 提供財政援助之聯邦機構
的公民權利辦公室 (office of civil rights) 提出第 VI 篇的投訴。

誰可以提出投訴？
第 VI 篇明令禁止歧視「任何人」。非美國國民也受到該法規的保護。

應提供的資訊
在向聯邦機構提出第 VI 篇投訴時，您應提供以下資訊：
  1.您的聯絡資訊 (例如電話號碼與地址)。
  a.若您代表他人提出申請，請提供您的姓名與聯絡資訊，以及您與此人的關係。
  2.所宣稱犯下歧視行為之聯邦財政援助的領受人。
  a. (例如交通部 (Department of Transportation))。
  3.說明所宣稱歧視行為及其日期。
  a. (例如)。
  4.說明所宣稱歧視行為導致特定不利影響的方式。
  a.不利影響是所宣稱歧視行為的負面自然結
  b. (例如)。
  5.說明不利影響對如何影響第 VI 篇所保護特定類別 (例如種族、膚色或國籍) 的個 人
  或團體。
  a.所謂不公平係指對「受保護的類別」與「未受保護的類別」造成不利影響 的
  比較。不公平主張為投訴的必要組成部分。
  b. (例如)。
  6.說明您可能因針對所宣稱歧視提出投訴而遭受的任何可能報復 (若有)。
  a.報復係指本機構基於您宣稱受到歧視而採取的任何不利行為。
  b. (例如)。
  7.投訴書必須簽名並標註日期。

   1964 년 Civil Rights Act(공민권법) 제 6 장(Title VI)에 따른
  이의 신청 안내

 제 6 장은 연방 자금 또는 기타 형태의 연방 금융 지원을 받는 프로그램 및 활동에서 인종, 피부
 색 및 출신 국가에 따른 차별을 금지하는 1964 년 공민권법의 일부입니다. 특히, 제 6 장은
 “미국에 있는 누구도 인종, 피부색 또는 출신 국가를 근거로 연방 금융 지원을 받는 모든 프로
 그램 또는 활동의 참여를 배제당하거나, 혜택을 받지 못하거나 혹은 차별의 대상이 되어서는 안
 된다”고 42 U.S.C. § 2000d 에 규정합니다. 연방 금융 지원을 받는 모든 프로그램 참여를 배
 제당하거나, 혜택을 받지 못하거나 혹은 차별의 대상이 되었다고 간주하는 경우, 금융 지원을 제
 공한 연방 기관 소속 민권담당국(Office for Civil Rights)에 제 6 장에 따른 이의를 제기할 수 있습
 니다.

누가 이의를 제기할 수 있나요?
제 6 장은 “사람(들)”의 차별을 금지합니다. 법령의 보호를 받는 사람이 미국 시민이어야 할 필요는
없습니다.

포함해야 하는 정보
연방 기관에 제기하는 제 6 장 이의는 다음 내용을 포함해야 합니다.

  1. 귀하의 연락처 정보(예: 전화번호, 주소)
  a. 다른 사람을 대신하여 이의를 제기하는 경우, 귀하의 성함, 연락처 정보 및 이의
  제기 신청자와의 관계를 포함해 주십시오.

  2. 차별 행위를 저지른 혐의가 있는 연방 금융 지원 수령자
  a. (예: 교통부(Department of Transportation))

  3. 차별 행위를 저지른 날짜를 비롯해 혐의와 관련된 설명
  a. (예:).

  4. 명시된 부정적 효과를 초래하는 데 차별 행위 혐의가 어떻게 영향을 미쳤는지 설명
  a. 부정적 효과란 차별 행위 혐의로 인한 자연스럽게 발생한 부정적 결과를 말합니
  다.
  b. (예:).

   5. 제 6 장이 보호하는 범위(예: 인종, 피부색 또는 출신 국가)를 근거로, 부정적
  결과가 개인 또는 집단에게 차별적인 영향을 미쳤는지 설명
  a. 차별이란 보호받는 계층과 보호받지 못하는 계층 사이에서 발생하는 부정적 결

  의 설명
  a. 차별 혐의 제기에 따라 독립체가 취한 부정적 행위와 관련된 보복 조치 내용

기간 내에 제기하는 것이 가장 좋습니다.

(NTS) Drug and Alcohol (D&A) Program Rules and Regulations. Subsequently, City Council has
approved amendments to this policy on various occasions including the current D&A Program
Rules and Regulations which were amended in February 2018 to reflect changes in federal
regulatory policy and procedures and NTS Rules and Regulations.

Staff is proposing to amend the Drug and Alcohol Program Rules and Regulations to comply
with Federal Transit Administration (FTA) guidelines and updates regarding covered employees
as it relates to the following:

(1) Section VIII - Covered Employees:

  a) Added the positions of Fleet Maintenance Supervisor and Mechanic Trainee to the list
  of safety- sensitive employees covered under this D A Program since these positions
  meet the definition by FTA regarding duties of these positions as it relates to maintaining
  transit vehicles used in revenue service.

  b) Removing Fleet Maintenance Manager and Manager Transit Operations from list of
  safety sensitive employees per FTA guidelines.

  a) A “Disclosure Statement” under Section IX has been added as a footnote to clarify
  that Assembly (AB) 2188, which amended California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act
  prohibiting employers from engaging in any adverse employment action against
  employees for off duty and away from the worksite use of marijuana, does not apply to
  Norwalk Transportation Department Safety-Sensitive employees (i.e. operating revenue
  vehicles, controlling dispatch of revenue vehicles, maintaining revenue vehicles, etc.).

  b) Pursuant to FTA guidelines, the Fleet Maintenance Manager and Manager of Transit

  included since they are directly involved with safety-sensitive job functions.

  c) The Designated Employee Representative for the D&A Program will change from Maria
  Barrera, Senior Human Resources Analyst, to Cecilia Hernandez, Payroll/Personnel
  Technician.

The IAMAW agreed with these recommended revisions to the D&A Program Rules and
Regulations.

I.  POLICY STATEMENT

  The City of Norwalk is committed to maintaining a safe and productive working
  environment. The City is also committed to providing reliable, courteous and
  efficient service to its bus patrons. The City recognizes the effect of substance
  abuse on safety and productivity and can cause a disruptive work environment.
  The City recognizes that safety-sensitive employees’ use of illegal drugs and
  misuse of alcohol poses a significant risk to public safety, as well as the
  employee’s health and well being.

  In keeping with this commitment, the City has adopted the Transportation
  Department’s Drug and Alcohol Program Rules and Regulations (“policy”) that
  is designed to:

  A.  create a work environment free from the adverse effects of drug abuse
  and alcohol misuse;

  B.  deter and detect employee’s use of illegal drugs and misuse of alcohol;

  C.  prohibit the unlawful manufacture, distribution, dispensing, possession,
  or use of controlled substances; and

  D.  encourage employees to seek professional assistance when personal
  problems, including drug and/or alcohol dependency, adversely affect his
  or her ability to safely perform duties assigned.

II.  PURPOSE

  The purpose of this policy is to ensure fitness for duty and to protect
  employees, passengers and the general public from the safety and health risks
  posed by the misuse of alcohol and the use of prohibited drugs. This policy is
  intended to comply with all applicable State and Federal laws and regulations
  governing workplace anti-drug use and alcohol misuse programs in the
  transportation industry. They include DOT 49 CFR Part 40, as amended
  (Procedures for Transportation Workplace Drug and Alcohol Testing Programs);
  49 CFR Part 655, as amended (Prevention of Alcohol Misuse and Prohibited
  Drug Use in Transit Operations); “Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988” (see
  Appendix C); and CA Govt. Code Section 8350, “Drug-Free Workplace Act of
  1990”. This policy incorporates the requirements of the above regulations for
  safety-sensitive employees.

  2
 III.  CONTACT PERSON

  The Designated Employer Representative (DER) authorized to receive test
  results and answer questions regarding the Transportation Department’s Drug
  and Alcohol Rules and Regulations is listed in appendix H.

  In case of DER’s absence, the Director of Transportation, will assign a
  designee, to receive test results and answer questions regarding this policy.

  Under the City’s Authority, the DER will be either a management classification
  or confidential personnel.

IV.  APPLICABILITY

  This policy applies to all City of Norwalk Transportation Department safety-
  sensitive employees, as defined in Section VIII of this policy. It applies to off-
  site lunch periods and breaks when an employee is scheduled to return to work
  or is on-call.

  All other City of Norwalk Transportation Department employees are covered by
  the City of Norwalk Drug and Alcohol-Free Work Environment Policy.

  Disclosure: Assembly Bill (AB) 2188, which is in effect as of January 1, 2024,
  amended California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), to prohibit
  employers from engaging in any adverse employment action against employees
  for off duty and away from the worksite use of marijuana. Exception: Federal
  Law Requires applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances
  (including marijuana).

  Further, this policy applies to any contractor who performs safety-sensitive
  functions and who “stands in the shoes” of the safety-sensitive employees of
  the City of Norwalk Transit System, unless the contractor has its own company
  policy that is FTA compliant with all applicable State and Federal regulations
  governing workplace anti-drug use and alcohol misuse programs in the
  transportation industry, in which case, their company policy will apply.

V.  PRE-EMPTION OF STATE AND LOCAL LAWS

  If any conflict occurs between State and local laws and regulation and any
  requirement of the above-mentioned Federal laws and regulations, the Federal
  laws and regulations prevail. However, Federal laws and regulations do not
  preempt provisions of State criminal laws that impose sanctions for reckless
  conduct attributed to prohibited drug use or alcohol misuse, whether the
  provisions apply specifically to transportation employees, employers, or the
  public in general.

VI.  DEFINITIONS

  A.  Adulterated Specimen
  3
   A urine specimen that contains a substance that is not expected to be
  present in human urine, or contains a substance expected to be present
  but is at a concentration so high that it is not consistent with human
  urine. Physical characteristics are outside normal range.

B.  Alcohol

  The intoxicating agent in beverage alcohol, ethyl alcohol or other low
  molecular weight alcohols, including methyl or isopropyl alcohol.

C.  Alcohol Use

  The drinking or swallowing of any beverage, liquid mixture or preparation
  (including medication) that contains alcohol. For purposes of this policy,
  alcohol is alcohol regardless of source.

D.  Breath Alcohol Technician (BAT)

  An individual who instructs and assists employees, applicants or
  transferees in the alcohol testing process and operates an Evidential
  Breath Testing (EBT) device.

E.  Canceled Test

  A drug or alcohol test that has a problem identified that cannot be or has
  not been corrected, or which Part 40 requires to be canceled. A
  canceled test is neither a positive nor a negative result.

F.  Collector

  A person who instructs and assists individuals at a collection site, who
  receives and makes an initial inspection of the specimen provided by the
  individual, and who initiates and completes the Custody and Control
  Form (CCF).

G.  Controlled Substance

  Any drug classified by the U. S. Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) into
  the five schedules or classes on the basis of their potential for abuse,
  accepted medical use, and accepted safety for use under medical
  supervision.

H.  Designated Employer Representative (DER)

  An employee or employees authorized by City of Norwalk Transit to take
  immediate action(s) to remove employees from safety-sensitive duties,
  or cause employees to be removed from such duties, following a positive
  test, test refusal, or other policy violations.

  4
 I.  Disabling Damage

  Damage which precludes departure of a motor vehicle from the scene of
  the accident in its usual manner in daylight after simple repairs, including
  damage to motor vehicles that could have been driven, but would have
  been further damaged if so driven.

  “Disabling damage” does not include:

  1.  Damage which can be remedied temporarily at the scene of the
  accident without special tools or parts;

  2.  Tire disablement without other damage even if no spare tire is
  available;

  3.  Headlamp or taillight damage; or

  4.  Damage to turn signals, horn, or windshield wipers, which makes
  them inoperative.

J.  DHHS

  Department of Health and Human Services

K.  DOT

  Department of Transportation

L.  Drug(s)

  The drugs for which tests are required under DOT and FTA regulations.
  They are marijuana, cocaine, amphetamines, phencyclidine (PCP) and
  opioids. This group of drugs is also referred to as the National Institute
  on Drug Abuse (NIDA) panel.

M.  Drug Abuse

  Use of any illegal drug or controlled substance without a valid
  prescription, misuse of legally prescribed drugs, or use of illegally
  obtained prescription drugs. This includes use of prescription drugs
  legally prescribed to another individual.

N.  Evidential Breath Testing (EBT) Device

  A device that is approved by the National Highway Traffic Safety
  Administration (NHTSA) for the evidential testing of breath at the .02 and
  .04 alcohol concentrations and appears on ODAPC's Web page for
  "Approved Evidential Breath Measurement Devices" because it conforms
  with the model specifications available from NHTSA.

  5
 O.  Alcohol Screening Device (ASD)

  A breath or saliva device, other than an EBT, that is approved by the
  National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and appears on
  ODAPC's web page for "Approved Screening Devices to Measure
  Alcohol in Bodily Fluids" because it conforms to the model specifications
  from NHTSA.

P.  FTA

  Federal Transit Administration

Q.  Invalid Drug Test

  The result of a urine drug test that contains an unidentified adulterant or
  an unidentified interfering substance, has abnormal physical
  characteristics, or has an endogenous substance at an abnormal
  concentration that prevents the laboratory from completing or obtaining a
  valid drug test result.

R.  Public Transportation

  Vehicles used to transport the public, whether in revenue service or not,
  or those used for ancillary services.

S.  Medical Review Officer (MRO)

  A licensed physician (medical doctor or doctor of osteopathy)
  responsible for receiving laboratory drug test results, who has knowledge
  of substance abuse disorders, and has the appropriate medical training
  to interpret and evaluate an individual’s confirmed drug and/or validity
  test results together with the individual’s medical history and any other
  relevant biomedical information. (See Appendix A for a detailed
  discussion of the MRO’s roles and responsibilities).

T.  Negative Dilute Specimen

  A specimen which contains no prohibited drug or the concentration of the
  drug is less than the cut off level, but the creatinine and specific gravity
  values are lower than expected for human urine. (See Section XV DRUG
  & ALCOHOL TESTING PROCEDURES for more information concerning
  re-tests).

U.  Alcohol Violation

  The presence of alcohol in the body at a concentration of 0.04 or greater
  as measured by an EBT device.

V.  Positive Drug Test

  6
   Any urine that is chemically tested (screened and confirmed), shows the
  presence of controlled substances, and is verified by the MRO.

W.  Refusal to Test

  Includes, but is not limited to, circumstances or behaviors such as:

  1.  Failure to appear at the collection site for any test in the time
  allotted. This excludes pre-employment testing for employment
  candidates, but includes safety-sensitive employees returning
  from a 90-day leave of absence;

  2.  Leaving the collection site before the testing process is
  completed, except in pre-employment situations where leaving the
  site before the testing process begins is not deemed to be a test
  refusal;

  3.  Failure or refusal to provide a urine or breath specimen as
  required by DOT Part 40;

  4.  Failure to permit the observation or monitoring of specimen
  collection when it is required;

  5.  Failure to provide a sufficient amount of urine or breath specimen
  without a valid medical explanation;

  6.  Failure or refusal to take a second test when required;

  7.  Failure to undergo a medical evaluation when required. (In the
  case of a pre-employment test, the individual is deemed to have
  refused to test only if the test is conducted following a contingent
  offer of employment.);

  8.  Failure to cooperate with any part of the testing process (e.g.,
  refusing to wash hands or empty pockets after being directed to
  do so by the collector, or behaving in a confrontational manner
  that disrupts the collection process);

  9.  Leaving the scene of the accident without just cause prior to
  submitting to a test;

  10.  If the MRO reports a verified adulterated or substituted test result;

  11.  Refuse to sign Step 2 of the Alcohol Testing Form;

  12.  An employee admits to the collector or MRO that he or she
  adulterated or substituted their specimen;

  13.  The employee fails to follow the observer’s instructions to raise
  and lower their clothing and to turn around to permit the observer
  7
   to determine if the employee has a prosthetic or other device that
  could be used to interfere with the collection process; or

  14.  The employee possesses or wears a prosthetic or other device
  that could be used to interfere with the collection process.

  Note:  A refusal to test carries the same consequences and
  disciplinary actions as a positive test result.

X.  Safety-Sensitive Employee

  As defined by the FTA, safety-sensitive employees include those who
  perform, are ready to perform, or may be called upon to perform, the
  following safety-sensitive functions:

  •  Operating a revenue service vehicle, even when it is not in
  revenue service.

  •  Operating a non-revenue service vehicle when required to be
  operated by a Commercial Driver’s License (CDL) holder;

  •  Controlling dispatch or movement of a revenue service vehicle;

  •  Maintaining (including repairs, overhaul and rebuilding) a revenue
  service vehicle or equipment used in revenue service.

Y.  Screening Test Technician (STT)

  A person who instructs and assists employees in the alcohol testing
  process and operates an alcohol screening device, such as a breath or
  saliva device other than an EBT.

Z.  Split Specimen

  In drug testing, a part of the urine specimen that is sent to a first
  laboratory and retained unopened, and which is transported to a second
  DHHS-certified laboratory for testing upon employee request following a
  verified positive or a verified adulterated or substituted test result form
  the primary specimen.

AA.  Substance Abuse Professional (SAP)

  A person who evaluates employees who have violated a DOT drug and
  alcohol regulation and makes recommendations concerning education,
  treatment, follow-up testing, and aftercare. (See Appendix C for a
  detailed discussion of the SAP’s roles and responsibilities.)

BB.  Substituted Specimen

  8
   A specimen with creatinine and specific gravity values that are so
  diminished that they are not consistent with human urine.

VII.  EDUCATION AND TRAINING

  The education and ongoing awareness component of this policy will include
  displaying posters, “Helpline Phone Numbers”, distributing the drug and alcohol
  policy and other informational materials to all employees, and periodic
  informational seminars.

  As required by FTA regulation, City of Norwalk Transportation Department will
  provide all safety-sensitive employees a minimum of 60 minutes of training on
  the effects and consequences of prohibited drug use on personal health, safety,
  the work environment, and on the signs and symptoms that may indicate
  prohibited drug use. See Appendix A for detailed information on the signs,
  symptoms, health effects and consequences of alcohol misuse.

  Supervisors or company officials who may make reasonable suspicion referrals
  shall receive a minimum of 60 minutes of training on the physical, behavioral
  and performance indicators of probable drug use, and at least 60 minutes of
  probable alcohol misuse.

VIII.  COVERED EMPLOYEES

  As a condition of employment, all covered employees are required to submit to
  drug and alcohol testing administered in accordance with 49 CFR Part 40 and
  49 CFR Part 655. A refusal to submit to a test as directed will be considered to
  be a positive test result and the employee will be subject to all the
  consequences stated in this policy. (See Section VI. DEFINITIONS for specific
  circumstances or behaviors that are considered refusal to test.)

  Covered employees include all safety-sensitive employees, as defined in
  Section VI of this policy. Using this definition, safety-sensitive employees
  include the following employee classifications:

  •  Fleet Maintenance Supervisor
  •  Lead Equipment Mechanic
  •  Equipment Mechanic
  •  Mechanic Trainee
  •  Equipment Service Worker
  •  Equipment Service Helper
  •  Transit Safety & Training Coordinator
  •  Senior Transit Operations Supervisor
  •  Transportation Operations Supervisor
  •  Transportation Operations Supervisor II
  •  Dispatcher
  •  Bus Operator (full-time & hourly/part-time)
  •  Bus Operator Trainee
